name: Cold spoons

lead: Cold spoons are spoons chilled in the freezer or fridge and held against the skin around the eyes to reduce puffiness. People use them for a quick, temporary de-puff, such as in the morning.

Cold is said to narrow blood vessels and reduce fluid in the tissue for a short time, so the area looks flatter. A general reference describes cold compression as sometimes recommended for swelling, with mixed evidence. Only a thin forum discussion of the spoon method exists, and no studies have tested it.

paras: People chill a metal spoon, hold the back against the closed eye area for a minute or two, and swap to a second spoon as the first warms. It is used as a morning routine step before skincare or makeup.
Ice or very cold metal directly on skin can cause cold burns, so a cloth barrier or briefer contact is common. Forum users also voice unverified nerve-damage worries.

angle.text: Forum posters press freezer-chilled spoons against the eye area to reduce puffiness. The cold narrows vessels and shifts fluid, so the under-eye looks flatter for a while. It is a home practice discussed in a few threads, with no published research.

lead: Cold spoons refers to pressing a spoon chilled in a freezer or fridge against the skin around the eyes to reduce puffiness or bloat. It is a home practice discussed in a few forum threads and has no published research behind it.

Looksmax.org users ask whether the method is legitimate, with one reply saying cold encourages blood flow and reduces swelling, and another thread participant recalling forum claims that ice can cause nerve damage. A general reference describes cold compression as sometimes recommended for swelling, with evidence that is mixed, and notes that ice applied directly to skin can cause burns.[1]

paras: The practice borrows from cold compresses: the cold object is held briefly against the eye area. Cold is described as narrowing blood vessels and reducing fluid leaking into tissue, presented as a short-term effect.[2]

Reference material on cold therapy reports that ice applied directly to skin can cause cold burns and that serious injuries have followed excessive cooling time with powered devices.[1] The reference does not mention nerve injury; the nerve-damage claim in forum discussion is not substantiated by the sources reviewed.
No studies found on cold spoons. Research on cold compression in sprains and post-surgical swelling is a different setting, and a review found insufficient evidence for acute ankle sprains.[1]
